html:
Sirimavo Bandaranaike of Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, was the first woman in the world to be elected prime minister. She took office on 21 July 1960 and held it three times.

She was born in 1916 into a family of Kandyan landowners. Her husband, S. W. R. D. Bandaranaike, became prime minister in 1956 on a wave of Sinhalese Buddhist feeling (see the Sinhala Only Act). A Buddhist monk shot him in 1959. His party asked his widow to lead it, and she won the next election.

Her governments, from 1960 to 1965 and 1970 to 1977, moved to the left. They took over the mission schools, the oil companies and the tea estates. Abroad she was a leader of the non-aligned countries.

She also pressed the majority's claims. Sinhala was enforced as the only language of government. In 1972 a new constitution made the country a republic, renamed it Sri Lanka and gave Buddhism the first place. Rules for entry to university cut the number of Tamil students. Tamil anger at these steps fed the civil war that came later. In 1971 she put down a rising of young Sinhalese Marxists at a cost of thousands of lives.

Her daughter became president in 1994 and made her prime minister once more. She died in 2000 on election day, just after voting.
